1:
No psalm in the first book carries a heading so contested, and the witnesses linger over "To the chief Musician upon Muth-labben" before the praise itself is heard. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the title so uncertain that he will not build on it: some refer Muth-labben to the death of Goliath, others of Nabal, others of Absalom, but he inclines to think it signifies only some tune or musical instrument to which the psalm was sung, taking the enemies here triumphed over to be the Philistines and the neighbouring nations subdued at the outset of David's reign. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers the ancient renderings into a heap: the Chaldee reads it "concerning the death of the strong man, or champion, who went out between the camps," that is, Goliath; the Vulgate, Septuagint, and Aethiopic, "concerning the secrets of the Son"; the Syriac and Arabic refer it to Christ's kingdom and resurrection; and Houbigant, uniting "al muth" into "alamoth," makes it "secret or hidden things." Clarke thinks the conjectures endless and declines to follow them all.

The reformed voices weigh the same riddle. John Calvin canvasses the theories - a chief captain among David's enemies, a fictitious name for Goliath, a musical instrument - but judges it more probable that Muth-labben was the opening of some well-known song to whose tune the psalm was set; and he insists the whole is to be read not as a bare song of victory but as a prayer, in which David recalls past deliverances to strengthen his confidence for present dangers. John Gill turns to the prayer itself, reading "I will praise thee, O Lord, with my whole heart" as the resolve to confess and declare openly the praises of God in the public congregation, the heart united and undivided, engaged with all its powers.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the psalm as the sequel to the eighth, an illustration of the divine name made glorious in the earth, and dismiss the guesses at the title as "curious conceits" sprung from a false division of the words, whether the Septuagint's "hidden things of the son," Luther's "lily-white youth," the Targum's Goliath, or the rabbinic reading of "labben" as a transposition for Nabal. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical witness, notes the feature that governs the whole poem: "the alphabetic arrangement is begun in its completest form," every clause of the first stanza opening with Aleph. The latin-fathers Augustine hears the title otherwise still, taking "the hidden things of the Son" of the only-begotten Son of God, for when Scripture says simply "the Son," without adding whose, the very excellency of the speaker gives him to be understood. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon leaves the heading for the resolve, hearing a holy determination to bless the Lord alone, with the whole heart, for "half heart is no heart," and to show forth to others all his marvellous works.
2:
The thanksgiving now names its true object, and the witnesses mark that David's gladness terminates not in the gift but in the Giver, "I will be glad and rejoice in thee." The reformed John Gill presses the point that the joy rests not in himself, in any attainment or warlike exploit, nor in second causes, horses and chariots and armies, but in the Lord as the God of all grace and his covenant God; and he notes the Chaldee's turn, "I will rejoice in thy Word," the essential Word of God so often typified under the former dispensation, adding that the two words heaped together here express a joy unspeakable and full of glory. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same lesson into a rule: whatever occurs to make us glad, our joy must pass through it and terminate in God only - "I will be glad and rejoice in thee, not in the gift so much as in the giver"; holy joy is the life of thankful praise as thankful praise is the language of holy joy, and both are fitly expressed by singing psalms. When God has shown himself above the proud enemies of the church, Henry adds, we must take occasion thence to give him glory as the Most High, and the triumphs of the Redeemer ought to be the triumphs of the redeemed.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the note personal and warm: "I am glad that thou hast heard my prayer, and showed me mercy; and I will rejoice in thee, in having thee as my portion, dwelling and working in my heart." The joy is not abstract gratitude but delight in a God possessed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar that binds this verse to the next, reading the coming clause "when mine enemies are turned back" with a preposition that carries at once the time and the reason - recedentibus hostibus meis retro, the foes driven backward - so that the singing to the name of the Most High rises directly out of the rout of the enemy, and the call to thanksgiving finds its ground in what God has done.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the praise here vowed is exultant and entire, fixed on God himself rather than on his benefits, and lifted to him under the very title, "O thou most High," by which the preceding psalm had celebrated his name as glorious in all the earth; the gladness is not in the deliverance so much as in the Deliverer, and it breaks into song only because it has first found its rest in him.
3:
From the vow of praise the ground of it comes into view, the rout of the foe, for when David's enemies "are turned back, they shall fall and perish at thy presence." The reformed John Gill reads the turning back through a widening lens - the Philistines fleeing when Goliath their champion fell, the officers who came to take David's antitype going backward and falling to the ground, and, in the last day, sin and Satan and the world and antichrist made to retreat before the Lord's people, who are more than conquerors through Christ. They shall stumble, Gill says, at whatever Providence throws in their way, and perish at the presence of God as wax melts before the fire, even as antichrist shall be consumed with the breath of Christ's mouth. This rout of the enemy, Gill adds, is the very ground and foundation of the psalmist's joy and singing, and will be the reason of the joy of the saints in the latter day. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the syntax, rendering the opening literally "in the turning of mine enemies back," which may mean either when they turned or because they turned; and he notes that the verb rendered "fall" is better "stumble through weakness," the Septuagint having "are weak," so that the second and third verses form a single sentence, the gladness breaking out as the enemy gives way.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the verse inward to the war with sin: it is a sure sign of a nearly won conquest when, by resistance, sin begins to lose its power; that is the time to follow on to know the Lord. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the doctrine of it: the almighty power of God is that which the strongest of his enemies can no way withstand; once they turn back they fall and perish, their very retreat their ruin, and they are saved no more by flying than by fighting. Henry hears the pattern fulfilled when the Lord Jesus, with the single word "I am he," made his enemies fall backward at his presence, as recorded in John 18:6, and could at the same moment have made them perish.

The witnesses do not divide. Whether the enemy be the Philistine host, the powers of hell, or the officers in the garden, they agree that the mere presence and glory of God suffices for the overthrow, and that to that presence, not to any instrument, the discomfiture is wholly to be ascribed; the enemy's flight is not their prudence but their ruin, and it is God, not David's sword, that turns them back.
4:
The reason for thanksgiving is now put as a matter of vindicated justice, God having sat in judgment on David's behalf, "thou hast maintained my right and my cause." The reformed John Gill reads it of a righteous cause vindicated and established, God having pleaded and defended it and, by the flight, fall, and ruin of his enemies, clearly made it appear that David's cause was just and good; for to him it belongs to sit in the throne and judge right. The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to both the wording and the structure. Charles Ellicott renders the clause literally "thou hast made my judgment," as the Septuagint and Vulgate have it, and finds in the confidence a match to Shakespeare's word in Henry the Eighth - "Heaven is above all yet; there sits a Judge that no king can corrupt" - a Judge set above all kings and past corrupting. Keil and Delitzsch mark that this strophe, opening with gimel, is perhaps meant to carry the daleth and he as well, and read the verse not as celebrating one recent judicial act alone but as the sum of many that went before, God sitting enthroned as the righteous Judge of the nations.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the throne its full weight: God sits in the throne of judgment, and to him it belongs to decide controversies, avenge the injured, and punish the injurious, for he has said, "Vengeance is mine"; to him it belongs to decide controversies, to determine appeals, and to render to every man according to his cause. We are sure, Henry adds, that the judgment of God is according to truth and that with him there is no unrighteousness; far be it from God that he should pervert justice. And if the present decisions of Providence seem to us to have some irregularity in them, that, instead of shaking our belief of God's justice, may serve to strengthen our belief of the judgment to come, which will set all to rights. Whoever disowns and deserts a just and injured cause, Henry concludes, we may be sure the righteous God will maintain it and plead it with jealousy, and never suffer it to be run down.

The witnesses do not divide. David's rescue is read as a single instance of a settled truth, that the God who fills the throne judges right, and that a righteous cause, though forsaken by men, is safe in his hands; the throne is no empty figure but the seat from which a real and present equity has already answered the psalmist's appeal.
5:
Three strokes of judgment are told in a breath, and the witnesses count them off, for God has "rebuked the heathen," "destroyed the wicked," and "put out their name for ever and ever." The reformed John Gill takes the heathen for the Philistines, or, as some Jewish writers, Amalek the chief of the nations, but refers the words chiefly to gospel times and the latter-day rebukes of the antichristian powers, whose utter extirpation shall issue in a profound peace among the churches. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the rebuke of the Canaanitish nations whom God destroyed from off the earth, and seizes on "for ever and ever," leolam vaed, as proof that olam here bears its proper endless sense: let the man who says it means only a limited time, Clarke challenges, tell us where the Hivites, Perizzites, and Jebusites now dwell, and when they are to be restored to Canaan; here, he says, olam keeps its proper signification, endless, without end. Gill for his part hears the rebuke of the antichristian powers coming with flames of fire and issuing in their utter extirpation, after which a profound peace and prosperity shall succeed in the churches.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens "put out" to "blotted out," the family extinct and its name erased from the civil register, as in Ps. 69:28 and Ps. 109:13; and he notes, in passing, a gap in the poem's alphabet - "the Daleth stanza is wanting," the acrostic skipping a letter here. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the three verbs as an ordered advance of divine power and justice against the enemies of the king newly set on Zion: God had first checked them, giving real proofs of his displeasure, that they might take warning by the rebukes of Providence and so prevent their own destruction; then he had cut them off, making some monuments of his vindictive justice; and last he had buried them in oblivion and perpetual infamy, blotting out their very name, that they should never be remembered with any respect.

The witnesses do not divide. Whether the nations be the old Canaanites, the Philistines, or the antichristian powers yet to fall, they read the verse as a total and final judgment, the erasing of a name that time itself will not recover; and Henry hears in the very warning of the rebuke that went before the destruction a mercy, a space in which the doomed might have turned and lived.
6:
"O thou enemy, destructions are come to a perpetual end" - the verse opens on a vocative so abrupt that the witnesses divide at once over whom it addresses and how it should be read. The reformed John Gill keeps the received address, though he passes over Goliath, of whom no destroyed cities are recorded, and the Jewish glosses on Esau and Amalek, to fix on antichrist, the great enemy of Christ and his church, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God, blaspheming the name of God, his tabernacle, and his saints. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry allows the words to be taken two ways - "Thou, O enemy, hast destroyed our cities," at least in intention, or "Thou, O God, hast destroyed their cities" - and presses on the enemy that their destruction is just, God reckoning with them for all the mischief done against his people, and that it is total and final, so devouring a thing is time that great and populous cities have been reduced to ruins whose very memorial has perished, while the saints look for a city that has stronger foundations.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott flatly refuses the vocative: "O thou enemy" gives no intelligible meaning; the line should run, "As for the enemy, they are made an utter wreck and perpetual ruin." The "destructions" he renders "desolations" or "ruins," from a root meaning to be dried up, and "their memorial" better "their very memory is perished," though the Septuagint and Vulgate read "with a sound," pointing to the crash of falling cities; Ellicott thinks the poet has in mind such an utter vanishing from history as befell Sodom, or the mounds that alone now mark Nineveh and Babylon. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, read the strophe as the sharp contrast on which the next verse turns, the enemies destroyed without a trace of remembrance while Jahve abides.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees with the correction, rendering "the enemy is desolated for ever; for thou hast destroyed their cities, and their memory is perished with them," and recalling how many cities of the Canaanites perished so utterly that neither name nor vestige remains. So the witnesses genuinely part over the grammar - whether David turns to taunt the enemy directly, or speaks of him in the third person as an utter wreck - while agreeing that the ruin described is complete, the very memory of the fallen swept from the earth.
7:
Against the vanished cities of the foe the psalm sets the one abiding throne, and the witnesses feel the contrast turn to comfort, "the Lord shall endure for ever." The reformed John Gill would render it "the Lord shall sit for ever," in rest and quiet when antichrist is wholly ruined, and hears in it the unchangeableness, eternity, and power of God; the Chaldee's "the Word of the Lord is for ever, his habitation in the highest heavens" he applies to Christ the essential Word, who sits at God's right hand until all his enemies are made his footstool. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the plain comfort: though cities and people perish, the Lord abides for ever, which is sufficient at once for the terror of his enemies and the comfort of his church. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the clause "Jehovah sits enthroned for ever," in close parallel with the next, "for judgment has erected his throne."

The puritan-evangelical witnesses dwell on the throne as the seat of a swift and certain justice. Matthew Henry comforts himself with three thoughts - God's eternity, on this earth nothing durable but the Lord ever the same and sitting even upon the floods unshaken, as in Ps. 29:10; his sovereignty, having prepared and fixed his throne by his infinite wisdom and immutable counsel; and his righteousness, ministering judgment to all persons and controversies in uprightness. It is the great support and comfort of good people, Henry says, when the power of the church's enemies is threatening and its affairs melancholy and perplexed, that God now rules the world and will shortly judge it. Charles Spurgeon hears in the prepared throne the swiftness of divine justice: in heaven's court suitors are not worn out with long delays, for "term-time lasts all the year round in the court of King's Bench above," and thousands may come at once to the Judge of all the earth without one complaint that their cause is not ready for a fair hearing.

The witnesses do not divide. The enduring existence and unchanging dominion of Jehovah, Spurgeon adds, are the firm foundations of the believer's joy - the enemy and his destructions come to a perpetual end, but God and his throne endure for ever. The eternity of the divine sovereignty, set over against the perishing of the enemy's cities, becomes the firm foundation of the believer's joy and the ground of an unhesitating confidence for all time to come; the same Almighty who has emptied the cities of the foe still fills the throne, and that throne is already made ready for judgment.
8:
The eternal throne is a throne of equity, and the witnesses take the verse as the charter of an impartial judgment, "he shall judge the world in righteousness." The reformed John Gill observes, with Ben Melech, that the word rendered "world" is a general name for all the countries of the habitable earth, so that a universal judgment is meant, carried on and finished with the utmost righteousness and the strictest equity - the very righteous judgment of God, in which every cause of every person shall be tried by an unerring rule. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lays a small stress on the pronoun, rendering "and he it is who shall minister judgment," the emphasis falling on the person of the Judge; and Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as widening the recent act of judgment into the prospect of a final one still more comprehensive, strict, and impartial, upon all the nations. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps it brief and broad: all the dispensations of God's providence are founded in righteousness and truth.

The puritan-evangelical voices press the comfort and the warning together. Matthew Henry hears God doing all every day, and about to do all at the last day, according to the eternal and unalterable rules of equity, ministering judgment to the people and determining their lot both in this world and in the future state, so that there shall not be the least colour of exception against his sentence. Charles Spurgeon turns the impartial tribunal upon the conscience: whatever earthly courts may do, heaven's throne ministers judgment in uprightness, for partiality and respect of persons are things unknown in the dealings of the Holy One of Israel; and the prospect of appearing before so even-handed a King should act at once as a check when we are tempted to sin and as a comfort when we are slandered or oppressed. The same throne, on his reading, that is the sinner's dread is the sufferer's security.

The witnesses do not divide. The judgment of the world is according to truth, and the certainty that God will do right is at once the reason a wronged man may leave his cause with him and the reason a guilty one should tremble; the same uprightness that clears the slandered condemns the proud, and no plea of place or person will bend it either way. It is the equity of the throne, not the fortune of the litigant, that decides.
9:
From the throne of judgment the psalm turns to the shelter it affords the weak, and the witnesses gather about the promise that God will be "a refuge for the oppressed." The reformed John Gill reads the oppressed as the poor and weak who have no might of their own, thrown down and trampled - God's people, oppressed with the burden of sin, pressed by Satan's temptations, trodden under foot by persecutors, yet finding the Lord their refuge; and, following the Chaldee's "Word of the Lord," he makes Christ the refuge typified by the cities of refuge, the strong tower and place of defence when all others fail, in the day of affliction, the hour of death, and at judgment. The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the imagery in the Hebrew. Charles Ellicott renders "refuge" properly "a stronghold," a citadel into which the persecuted would retreat, "oppressed" as "crushed," and "trouble" from a root meaning to be cut off - from provisions, water, and the like, its cognate in Jer. 14:1 meaning "drought." Keil and Delitzsch add that the word for stronghold, a high steep place where one is removed from danger, was a figure familiar to David from his time of persecution, and that the "crushed" one is he who is overwhelmed to the point of being wholly broken in pieces.

The puritan-evangelical voices draw the pastoral comfort. Matthew Henry notes that it is the lot of God's people to be oppressed in this world and to have troublous times appointed them, and that though God may not immediately appear as their deliverer, they may by faith flee to him as their refuge, a high and strong place, and depend on his power and promise so that no real hurt shall be done them. Charles Spurgeon sets the two halves of the psalm side by side: he who gives no quarter to the wicked in the day of judgment is the defence and refuge of his saints in the day of trouble; there were cities of refuge under the law, and under the gospel God himself is our refuge-city.

The witnesses do not divide. The God who judges the nations is the stronghold of the crushed, and the very severity that undoes the oppressor is the safety of the oppressed; the same throne that is terror to the persecutor is a high tower to the persecuted, who has only to flee into it to be safe.
10:
Trust grows out of knowledge, the verse says, and the witnesses trace the chain from knowing God's name to seeking his face, "they that know thy name will put their trust in thee." The reformed John Gill takes the name known as God proclaimed in the gospel, gracious and forgiving, and as the name of Christ himself, the able, willing, all-sufficient Saviour, known not merely notionally but affectionately, spiritually, and experimentally. The wesleyan-arminian voices read the knowledge as tested experience. Adam Clarke: those who have an experimental acquaintance with God's mercy will trust in him, convinced that he never has forsaken and never will forsake them that trust in him. John Wesley glosses the name as God's infinite power, wisdom, faithfulness, and goodness, and grounds the confidence on the experience of his dealings with his people in all ages.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the name as a watchword of strength and protection, and "seek" from a root meaning to tread or frequent a place, perhaps with allusion to frequenting the courts of the temple. Keil and Delitzsch hear in the verse the throb of a great missionary idea even in this early Davidic psalm - that Jahve's salvation shall be proclaimed from Zion to all the world, outside Israel, for their salvation. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the whole as a graded certainty: the better God is known the more he is trusted, for those who know him to be of infinite wisdom will trust him further than they can see him, as in Job 35:14, and those who know his almighty power will trust him when all creature-confidences fail, as in 2 Chron. 20:12; the more God is trusted the more he is sought unto; and God never did, nor ever will, disown or desert any that duly seek him and trust in him. Those who know him to be a God of inviolable truth and faithfulness, Henry continues, will rejoice in his word of promise and rest upon it though its performance be deferred, and those who know him to be the Father of spirits and an everlasting Father will trust him with their souls, as their main care, at all times, even to the end.

The witnesses do not divide. Knowledge breeds trust, and trust breeds seeking, and the seeker is met by a God who has never once forsaken those who came to him; the grace that assures David of this is, as Henry notes, the same grace in all the saints, so that what he has found the least of them may find too.
11:
The single voice of praise now summons a choir, and the witnesses hear David turn from his own resolve to a call upon others, "sing praises to the Lord, which dwelleth in Zion." The reformed John Gill notes that the word rendered "sing praises" means a modulation of the voice in musical notes - the same word used elsewhere of the singing of birds - and that this is a work for the saints jointly, in concert together, as Paul and Silas sang in prison, since they share the blessings of grace in common and ought to stir one another up to it. The Lord is not only to be praised, Gill adds, by celebrating the perfections of his nature and the works of his hands, by giving thanks for mercies temporal and spiritual, and by living to his glory, but his very praises are to be sung. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the dwelling-place: as the special residence of God's glory is in heaven, so the special residence of his grace is in his church, of which Zion was a type, where he meets his people with his promises and they should meet him with their praises; and David commands his own subjects and courts his neighbours to sing, not, as hitherto, to their false gods, but to the God of Israel, and to own among the heathen the great things he has done for his people.

The wesleyan-arminian voices take up the second clause, "declare among the people his doings." Adam Clarke makes it the duty of all who have received God's salvation to recommend him and his salvation to the whole circle of their acquaintance, and laments that Christians so seldom speak of God when they meet - because, he says bluntly, they have nothing to say. John Wesley reads "the people" as the heathen nations, and "which dwelleth in Zion" of the God whose special and gracious presence is there. In all our praises, Henry urges, we should have an eye to God as dwelling in Zion, in a special manner present in the assemblies of his people as their protector and patron.

The witnesses do not divide. The praise that began in one grateful heart is meant to spread through the assembly and out among the nations, sung to the God who has fixed his gracious presence in Zion and published there among the peoples the record of his doings; those who believe God is greatly to be praised, Henry adds, not only desire to do that work better themselves, but would gladly bring others to join them in it.
12:
The praise is grounded in a solemn assurance about shed blood, and the witnesses weigh what it means that God "maketh inquisition for blood." The reformed John Gill takes the searching as God's own: he knows where the blood of his saints lies, though ever so privily shed, as he did Abel's, and is represented as seeking it out that he may demand satisfaction, requiring the blood of every man at the hand of him by whom it is shed, and especially the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the phrase "the seeker of bloods," that is the goel, the avenger of blood, the nearest relative who by Oriental custom must avenge the murdered man; and he would put the verbs in the past - "remembered," "forgot not" - the sufferers being the afflicted about to be named. Keil and Delitzsch read the strophe as the recollection of how the humble had cried to God before the deliverance now enjoyed, the tremulous, resolved form of "have mercy" designedly chosen.

The wesleyan-arminian voices widen and steady the sense. Adam Clarke applies the inquisition not only to the Canaanites and Philistines who shed the blood of God's people but to all the nations of the earth who, for wealth or empire, have made destructive wars; for the blood such nations have unjustly spilt, their own shall be required, and the cry of the peoples driven to ruin is not forgotten before God. John Wesley glosses the blood as that of God's innocent and holy ones, which, though he seem not to regard it for a season, he will certainly call the authors of it to a severe account. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the day of inquisition against the day of the great judgment: God remembers every drop of innocent blood and will return it sevenfold, as he promised in Deut. 32:43 to avenge the blood of his servants, and it will then appear that he has not forgotten the cry of the humble, neither the cry of their blood nor the cry of their prayers, but that both are sealed up among his treasures.

The witnesses do not divide. The God who seems to overlook the oppressor's violence is in truth its unforgetting avenger, and the silent blood of his people is safe in his remembrance, kept, as Henry says, among his treasures against the day when he makes inquisition for it.
13:
After the confidence, a cry: the psalmist turns from the assembly's praise to his own need and pleads, "Have mercy upon me, O Lord." The reformed John Gill observes that a man called by grace, though he has already obtained mercy, still needs fresh discoveries of it, merciful supplies and support and deliverances; and such a one flees not to the creature but to God, pleading not his own dignity or merit but the mercy of God alone. The puritan-evangelical voices dwell on the humility and the hope of the prayer. Matthew Henry has David beg first that God would be compassionate - "have mercy upon me, who, having misery only, and no merit, to speak for me, must depend upon mercy for relief" - and then that he would consider his trouble, submitting the request to God's wisdom without prescribing the remedy; and he hears David plead the malice of his enemies and the experience of past succours in the title "O thou that liftest me up from the gates of death," for we are never brought so low but God can raise us up. Charles Spurgeon calls the opening petition "a little prayer-book," having in it the very soul and marrow of prayer, multum in parvo; and he glories in the title given the Most High, "thou that liftest me up from the gates of death," quoting Trapp's quaint word that God "commonly reserveth his hand for a dead lift, and rescueth those who were even talking of their graves." The petition, Spurgeon notes, breathes a humble spirit, indicates self-knowledge, and appeals to the proper attributes and to the fitting person, for between praising and praying David divided all his time.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the gates of death as an open grave leading to a yawning hell, and the answering gates of the daughter of Zion as all the ordinances by which the soul is helped forward to heaven. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note the resolved, tremulous form of the verb "have mercy" and the vocative "thou that liftest me up," and take the gates of death for the gates of the realm of the dead.

The witnesses do not divide. The same man who has just proclaimed God the refuge of the crushed now casts himself, with nothing but his misery and God's mercy to plead, upon the hand that lifts the dying from the very gates of the grave; and his aim, as the next verse will show, is not his own ease but the praise he means to render when he is raised.
14:
The plea for mercy carries its own purpose, and the witnesses hear David ask deliverance not for his own credit but for God's praise, "that I may shew forth all thy praise in the gates of the daughter of Zion." The reformed John Gill reads "all thy praise" as all the bounties and acts of divine goodness deserving of praise, even as many of them as he had an experience of and was capable of observing; for otherwise, Gill grants, the instances of divine grace and goodness are so many that they cannot be reckoned up in order, nor God be fully praised for them in the present state of things as he should. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the motive: "Lord, save me, not that I may have the comfort and credit of the deliverance, but that thou mayest have the glory, that I may show forth all thy praise, and that publicly"; and the place of the praise, the gates of the daughter of Zion, is that same Zion where God was said to dwell, so that David would attend him there with joy in his salvation - a salvation typical, Henry adds, of the great salvation to be wrought out by the Son of David.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fixes the imagery: the gates are the great assemblies, elegantly opposed to the gates of death of the verse before, and "the daughter of Zion" names the people who live and meet together in Zion, for cities are as it were mothers to their inhabitants and the people commonly called their daughters, as the daughters of Egypt and of Edom stand for their peoples. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the church's confidence that it will yet praise God in Zion's gates, rescued from the death that its enemies had wished upon it, and rejoicing in his salvation, the very deliverance it had cried for now turned into the matter of its song.

The witnesses do not divide. The deliverance asked is asked for the sake of the praise it will bring, the rescued man vowing to carry his joy from the gates of death to the gates of Zion, and there to publish, as far as mortal thanks can reach, all the salvation of his God; the lift from the grave is desired that it may become a song in the congregation, and the rescue an occasion of glory to the Rescuer.
15:
The praise David vowed becomes a picture of retribution, the trap sprung on its own maker, "the heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made." The reformed John Gill, following Jarchi and Aben Ezra, takes this very scene for "the praise" he had resolved to show forth, occasioned by the destruction of God's enemies and the deliverance of his people; the metaphor, he says, is from hunters who dig pits for the wild beasts to fall into, and he reads it prophetically of the nations that join the idolatry of antichrist and are brought to ruin by the very design with which they thought to destroy the kingdom of Christ. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply refers the reader to the same figure in the seventh psalm, Ps. 7:16, and Keil and Delitzsch fix the Hebrew verb, "to sink in," the wicked pressed down into the very net they had hidden, their own foot caught.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke points back to his note on Ps. 7:15, where the covered pit disguised with reeds figures the plotter undone by his own scheme. The puritan-evangelical voices press the moral and mark the pause. Matthew Henry reads it as God executing judgment so as to shame the wicked and make their fall inglorious, sunk in the pit they digged, as in Ps. 7:15, and snared in the work of their own hands - for the overruling providence of God frequently orders it that persecutors are brought to ruin by the very projects they meant to be destructive, so that drunkards kill themselves and the contentious bring mischief upon themselves. Charles Spurgeon, held by the untranslated words that follow, bids the reader pause and meditate: like cunning hunters the heathen prepared a pitfall for the godly and fell into it themselves, the foot of the victim escaping while the toils surrounded the trapper, the cruel snare proving its efficacy by snaring its own maker. Persecutors and oppressors, he adds, are often ruined by their own malicious projects, so that men's sins may be read in their punishment and the destruction of sinners appears to be, not only meritoriously but efficiently, of themselves.

The witnesses do not divide. The judgment needs no thunderbolt, for the wicked man's own spade and his own weight bring him down into the grave he had dug for another; the very hands that laid the net are the hands that are caught in it.
16:
What the pit displayed, this verse states as a revelation of God's character, "the Lord is known by the judgment which he executeth." The reformed John Gill reads the judgment upon antichrist and the antichristian powers as the very means of making God's name and glory, his wisdom, power, justice, and goodness, known in all the earth, a just retaliation in which the persecutor is repaid in his own coin - as he killed with the sword he shall be killed with the sword, and as he burned the martyrs of Jesus he shall be cast into the lake of fire. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the clause "Jehovah hath made himself known: he hath executed judgment, snaring the wicked in the work of his own hands," and Keil and Delitzsch hear the grateful retrospect passing over into a confident view of a future thereby guaranteed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds that the Lord makes himself known by these judgments - it is known that there is a God who judges in the earth, a righteous God who hates sin, so that in them the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all unrighteousness.

Then comes the pair of untranslated words, "Higgaion. Selah," and over Higgaion the witnesses divide. The puritan-evangelical Henry takes it as a note extraordinary, commanding special regard, a thing to be carefully observed and meditated upon, both the present judgments we see and the judgment to come. The wesleyan-arminian voices lean the same way while allowing the other: Adam Clarke first reads "Higgaion, Selah" as "Meditate on this; mark it well," yet grants that some make it a direction to the musicians, like our Presto or Largo, to play briskly and boldly; John Wesley calls it either a musical term or a note of attention intimating that the matter deserves deep meditation. The grammatical-historical Ellicott holds both possibilities open: Higgaion occurs three times in the Psalter, translated "meditation" in Ps. 19:14 and "solemn sound" in Ps. 92:3, both senses etymologically possible, so that the word marks either a change in the music or a call to ponder.

The witnesses do not finally divide over the doctrine - that God is known by his judgments and the sinner caught in his own devices - but only over whether the marginal word bids the orchestra sound or the soul consider; and even those who read it musically grant that the music is meant to deepen the meditation it accompanies.
17:
"The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God" - the most quoted line of the psalm, and the one over which the witnesses most sharply divide, for its first word is a crux. The reformed John Gill notes that some render it "shall return to the grave," to the dust from which they came; but since that is common to the righteous too, he takes it rather of the place of torment, hell, whither the souls of the wicked go, and where, after the judgment, the beast and false prophet shall be cast into the lake of fire. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the strong sense and heightens it: the original lisholah is very emphatic, "headlong into hell, down into hell"; and the nations that forget God are those who, though they know him, are unmindful of him in their designs and works, and are all to be thrust down. John Wesley glosses the forgetting as not regarding God, his precepts, or his threatenings.

Against this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the other reading hard, calling "shall be turned into hell" "a most unfortunate rendering." The true translation, he argues, is "the wicked shall return to the grave," that is to the dust, according to the doom of Gen. 3:19, or to the unseen world, as in Job 30:23; the verbs may even be imperative, "let them return," as in the Septuagint and Vulgate. Yet he grants an intensity in the original word lisheolah, with its double sign of direction, "right down to the world of death." Keil and Delitzsch read it likewise as the return to dust, the redactio in pulverem, man formed from the dust going back to it.

The puritan-evangelical voices keep the doctrine of judgment without settling the philology. Matthew Henry hears the wicked turned into hell as captives into a prison-house, forgetfulness of God being the cause of all their wickedness, and their multitude no security. Charles Spurgeon warns that not only the openly profane but the forgetters of God - the moral who are not devout, the amiable who are not converted - must have their portion in the nethermost hell. So the witnesses genuinely part: whether the line consigns the wicked to a place of torment, or, more soberly, returns them to the dust and the world of the dead - while all agree that to forget God is itself to be lost.
18:
Over against the doom of the godless the psalm sets a promise to the destitute, and the witnesses hear the accent fall on the words "not alway," for "the needy shall not alway be forgotten." The reformed John Gill takes the needy for God's people, poor in temporal things and poor in spirit, whose wants are many; strictly they are never forgotten, being engraven on God's hands and set as a seal on his heart, yet they may seem to be forgotten, both to themselves and others, and may lie long under affliction while the holy city is trodden under foot, the witnesses prophesying in sackcloth and the church kept in the wilderness for her appointed season. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the syntax that carries the comfort: in the original the negative stands emphatically at the head, ruling both clauses, as in Ps. 35:19; and "the expectation of the poor" is the sufferer's hope of being righted, which will at some time be realised. Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the confident turn by which, on the strength of the judgment already witnessed, the psalmist looks to the deliverance still to come.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the plain assurance: the needy and the poor, whose expectation is from the Lord, are never finally forgotten, though their deliverance be delayed for the greater confusion of their enemies and the greater manifestation of God's mercy. The puritan-evangelical voices steady the waiting soul. Matthew Henry encourages God's people to wait for a salvation that may be long deferred: the needy may think themselves forgotten and their expectation perished, but he that believes does not make haste, for the vision is for an appointed time; God will not only remember them at last but make it appear he never did forget them, for it is impossible he should, though a woman may forget her sucking child. Charles Spurgeon adds that Satan tells poor tremblers their hope shall perish, but here is divine assurance that their expectation shall not perish for ever, so that they may have to wait, but shall find they do not wait in vain.

The witnesses do not divide. The seeming forgetfulness is only seeming and only for a time, and the hope of the crushed is safe with a God who cannot finally forget his own; what looks to the sufferer like abandonment is, on the psalm's showing, a deferral with an appointed end.
19:
The confidence of the promise turns at once into petition, and the witnesses hear the psalm close by pleading that man not be suffered to overtop his Maker, "Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail." The reformed John Gill reads the cry as a call for God to rise to the destruction of his enemies and the salvation of his people. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens "let not man prevail" to "let not mere man be defiant," the word for man denoting frail mortal man; and Keil and Delitzsch note that David's "Arise, O Lord" is taken from the lips of Moses in Num. 10:35, a summons to God to appear and take part in a history from which he has seemed to withdraw into repose - and that the verb does not mean "let not man become strong," as some render, but let him not feel and act as though possessed of power.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as a prayer that this may be the time God will deliver his poor people under oppression and persecution. The puritan-evangelical voices give the petition its edge. Matthew Henry hears David pray that God would restrain the proud enemies of his church and set bounds to their malice - "let not man prevail; consult thy own honour, and let not weak and mortal men prevail against the kingdom of the almighty and immortal God. Shall mortal man be too hard for God, too strong for his Maker?" - and that he would reckon with them, letting the heathen be judged in his sight and called to account for the dishonour done to his name; for impenitent sinners will be punished in God's sight, and when their day of grace is over the bowels even of infinite mercy will not relent toward them. Charles Spurgeon calls prayers the believer's weapons of war: when the battle is too hard for us we call in our great ally, who lies as it were in ambush until faith gives the signal by crying "Arise, O Lord," and though our cause be all but lost it shall soon be won if the Almighty do but bestir himself.

The witnesses do not divide. The psalm that trusted God to judge the nations now begs him to do it, and the whole plea rests on the absurdity of frail, mortal man setting himself against the immortal God; the very name for man in the verse, they agree, is the argument, that a creature so weak should never be allowed to prevail.
20:
The last verse asks only that the nations be made to feel their own frailty, and the witnesses hear the psalm end where pride is broken, "Put them in fear, O Lord: that the nations may know themselves to be but men." The reformed John Gill reads it of a bold, impudent, fearless generation that neither fears God nor regards men, and prays that God, who alone can do it, would inject fear into them, as he will at the last overthrow of Babylon when her kings and merchants stand afar off for fear of her torment. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears David pray God to strike a terror upon them, for God knows how to make the stoutest of men tremble and flee when none pursues, and thereby to make them own that they are but men - weak men, unable to stand before the holy God, sinful men whose guilty consciences make them subject to alarms; it is a desirable thing, much for the glory of God, that men should know and consider themselves to be but men, depending, mutable, mortal, and accountable creatures. Charles Spurgeon marvels that men should ever grow so vain as to deny themselves to be but men, when crowns and learning and conquest and all the wealth of Croesus leave their possessor but a man.

But the reading itself is disputed, and here the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke parts from the received text. The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Syriac, he shows, read "place a lawgiver, or teacher, over them" - shithah morah lahem - so that the prayer becomes, with Coverdale, "O Lord, set a Schoolmaster over them," that they may learn they are accountable creatures and grow wise unto salvation; the word "teacher or legislator," he says, is the reading of all the versions but the Chaldee, though several manuscripts read morre, "fear." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the difficulty: the ancient versions read "place a lawgiver or master over them," Hitzig conjectures "set a guard upon them," while the present reading yields "put a terror upon them," such a proof of power as to trouble and subdue them.

Clarke marks the closing "Selah" as a call to mark well what is said, and records Bishop Horsley's division of the whole psalm into three parts - a prophetic song of victory over the persecuting faction, an exhortation to praise mixed with supplication and complaint, and a cool closing assertion of the ruin of the wicked and the deliverance of the saints. The witnesses part over the word - whether David asks God to terrify the nations or to set a teacher over them - but agree on the end in view, that proud mortals be brought, one way or another, to know themselves but men.
